    • Support and resistance

    Fibonacci retracement levels: the ratios of a move

    The Fibonacci retracement tool splits the move between a swing low and a swing high into ratios. The levels show how much of that move price has given back; the 0.618 level is where 61.8% of the move has been given back. The same tool also shows extensions beyond the move.

    What is a Fibonacci retracement?

    A trend makes pullbacks along the way. The Fibonacci retracement tool is drawn between the start and the end of the last move and splits that range into ratios. Each level shows how much of the move price has given back: 0.5 half of it, 0.618 61.8% of it.

    The ratios are named after the Fibonacci sequence. 0.618 corresponds to the ratio of successive numbers in the sequence (the golden ratio), and 0.382 and 0.786 to values derived from it. 0.5 is not a Fibonacci ratio, but it is on the tool because it is the exact middle of the move.

    How is it drawn?

    Each step gives the bullish (rising) move first, then the bearish (falling) move.

    1. Choose the move Pick a move between a clear swing low and swing high, preferably one that broke structure (BOS or CHoCH). The levels are calculated from these two points.
    2. Anchor the ends For a bullish move the tool is drawn from the low to the high: 1 at the swing low, 0 at the swing high. For a bearish move it is drawn from the high to the low: 1 at the swing high, 0 at the swing low.
    3. Read the levels The levels in between fall into place on their own. The retracement levels sit below the high for a bullish move and above the low for a bearish move; the extensions lie beyond 0, in the direction the move would continue.

    Commonly used levels

    • 0.236 and 0.382: a shallow pullback. In strong trends price often comes this far and moves on.
    • 0.5: the exact middle of the move. The same idea as a range's EQ (equilibrium) line; in a bullish move the upper half is called the premium area and the lower half the discount area, the other way round in a bearish move.
    • 0.618, 0.702 and 0.786: the deep pullback band. Some sources call this band OTE (optimal trade entry). Most of the move has been given back, but its start still holds.
    • 1: the start of the move. A close beyond this level shows that the move has been fully given back; a break of the swing low in a bullish move, of the swing high in a bearish one.

    Extensions

    Extensions fall beyond the move's 0 point, in the direction it would continue.

    • −0.27: 27% of the move beyond it. Equal to the distance between 0 and 0.28.
    • −0.618: 61.8% of the move beyond it. Equal to the distance between 0 and 0.618.
    • −1: one full move beyond it; twice the move when measured from the start. Also called a measured move.

    Extensions are not targets but a scale reference for the size of the move. Price can turn before reaching these distances or go much further.

    Where does the pullback stop?

    When price pulls back into the levels, one of three pictures usually follows. Each card covers the bullish and bearish move together.

    Shallow pullback

    Price turns before reaching 0.382 and moves beyond 0; a new high in a bullish move, a new low in a bearish one. This can point to a strong trend.

    Deep pullback

    Price comes as far as the 0.618–0.786 band but does not close beyond 1. The start of the move holds; structure is intact.

    Move given back

    A candle closes beyond 1; below the swing low in a bullish move, above the swing high in a bearish one. The levels lose their meaning; structure may have changed (see CHoCH).

    Reading the levels together with other marks

    On its own a Fibonacci level is only a ratio. It means more when it lines up with an order block, a supply or demand zone, an FVG, an earlier support or resistance zone or a trendline. Different methods pointing to the same price is called confluence; the more marks meet in the same place, the more the level stands out.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • How much of the move a pullback has given back
    • Whether the start of the move still holds
    • Reference levels that many people watch

    What it does not prove

    • That Fibonacci ratios are a natural law of price movement
    • That price will turn at a particular level
    • Which low and high should be chosen; different choices give different levels

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    In MarketLevelMap's Price Action view Fibonacci is shown by these rules.

    • The levels are drawn on the structure's current leg; 1 at the protected low or high, 0 at the leg extreme. Nothing is shown when the structure is undetermined.
    • The Fibonacci row in the Structure table says how much of the leg price has given back (for example "62% · deep band") and shows the price range of the 0.618–0.786 band.
    • The eye in that row turns the band and the 0, 0.5 and 1 lines on and off on the chart; it is off by default.
    • The EQ line in the Price Action view is the range's 0.5 level. The panel's "price at …% of the range" also shows where price sits in the range as a ratio.
    • The premium and discount words in the same panel say whether price is in the upper or lower half of the range.

    The choice is subjective

    On the same chart different people can choose different lows and highs, and the levels change with them. Levels drawn on clear swings of a larger timeframe are seen by more people. A level is read together with the move and timeframe it was drawn on.

    Often confused with

    • Pullback or reversal?Fibonacci levels measure how deep a pullback is; whether the pullback turns into a reversal is decided by structure (the protected low or high).
    • Ranges and consolidationA range's EQ line is a 0.5 level drawn between the range's high and low.
    • Psychological levels: why round numbers matterPsychological levels are round prices; Fibonacci levels are ratios of a chosen move.

    Key points

    • The levels show how much of the last move price has given back.
    • Drawn from low to high for a bullish move, from high to low for a bearish one; 1 is the start, 0 the end.
    • 0.618–0.786 is the deep pullback band; a close beyond 1 gives the move back.
    • The ratios are not a law; they gain meaning when read together with other marks.
